content:
I'm trying to figure out how to use docs#DihedralGroup.

import Mathlib.GroupTheory.SpecificGroups.Dihedral

open scoped Pointwise RightActions in
example (H : Subgroup (DihedralGroup 4))
    (h1 : H = Subgroup.zpowers (DihedralGroup.r 1))
    : H.Normal := by
  let D₄ := DihedralGroup 4
  rw [normal_iff_eq_cosets]
  have h₀ : (1 : D₄) •> H.carrier =
      {DihedralGroup.r 0, DihedralGroup.r 1,
       DihedralGroup.r 2, DihedralGroup.r 3} := by
    ext x
    apply Iff.intro
    · intro hx
      have h5 : Fintype D₄ := DihedralGroup.instFintypeOfNeZeroNat
      fin_cases hx

      done
    · intro hx
      done
    done
  done

For our purposes here, I specifically want to show that (1 : D₄) •> H.carrier is contained in the literal set I've typed out by applying Set.ext (as I've done) and then breaking down the expression (1 : D₄) •> H.carrier into the four possible cases 1 * some_rotation for each of the four rotations in H.carrier. (I'm hoping, since each element of the zpowers subgroup ends up being defined by a ZMod, that Lean already realizes H.carrier is finite.)

h5 was my attempt to get fin_cases to work, which it isn't doing. What do I need to do?

(I'm not attached to using the fin_cases tactic specifically. That was just what came up when I searched for how to do a general proof by cases over a finite list of possibilities.)

What do you expect fin_cases hx to do?

Does simp do what you expect it to do?

Well, what fin_cases hx is doing is generating an error.

What I want it to do is give me four cases, in which hx gets replaced by hypotheses x = DihedralGroup.r 0, x = DihedralGroup.r 1, x = DihedralGroup.r 2, and x = DihedralGroup.r 3. The 0, 1, 2, and 3 should be values of type ZMod 4.

By the way, have h5 : Fintype D₄ := DihedralGroup.instFintypeOfNeZeroNat is never right. Firstly, Fintype is data not a proof (it's a list of the elements, not a proof that there are only finitely many) so you should use let not have (in fact I am quite surprised that there is no linter getting upset about this). Secondly, let h5 : Fintype D₄ := inferInstance also works, which means that the typeclass inference system already knows that D_4 is finite, which means that the line isn't doing anything.
simp does what I expect, inasmuch as it applies a theorem that 1 •> s = s for all s, but that's not what I want to do here.

Like I said, I'm not attached to using fin_cases. I want to know how to break the assumption "x belongs to this finite set" into cases defined by the elements of the set. No different from using cases on a logical disjunction.
Is cases x what you are looking for?

simp [h1, mem_zpowers_iff_mem_range_orderOf] at hx changes it to hx : ∃ a < 4, DihedralGroup.r ↑a = x.

      simp [h1, mem_zpowers_iff_mem_range_orderOf] at hx
      obtain ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩ := hx
      interval_cases a

will give you your 4 goals. The reason fin_cases doesn't work is explained in the error: the hypothesis is not of the form "x is in a list" or "x is in a finset" or "x is in a multiset", it's "x is in a subgroup".

Damiano Testa said:

Is cases x what you are looking for?

Not unless you know something I don't. That's very possible, but if so you haven't mentioned it.

It's not looking good, though, because cases x includes a case where x is generated by DihedralGroup.sr, which (a) is impossible; and (b) will prevent the proof from compiling, since it will ultimately rely on the fact that that isn't the case.
Why would it prevent the proof from compiling? You just need to prove that case is impossible.

Kevin Buzzard said:

The reason fin_cases doesn't work is explained in the error: the hypothesis is not of the form "x is in a list" or "x is in a finset" or "x is in a multiset", it's "x is in a subgroup".

What? That can't be true; it's of the form "x is in a set". 1 •> H.carrier is a pointwise operation on a set that produces another set. Subgroups never enter into it. (And boy, working with cosets of subgroups is incredibly annoying for this very reason!)
It happens that the set x is in is a set of a Fintype, so I was assuming that there was a Finset derivation available.

Aaron Liu said:

Why would it prevent the proof from compiling? You just need to prove that case is impossible.

Fair enough. That still isn't the method I was hoping to learn about. I want "x is in this set of four elements, so let's look at four cases", not "x is in this set that is a subset of a set of eight elements, so let's look at all eight possible cases".

Michael said:

What? That can't be true; it's of the form "x is in a set".

Sorry, simp turned it into x \in H. But my point still stands. The goal is "x is in a Set", not "x is in a Finset or List or Multiset". These things are disjoint in type theory.
So... the 'correct' approach here is to define a Finset that's equal to 1 •> H.carrier, and use fin_cases on that?
Do you have any words of wisdom on why inferring a Fintype works and is good, but inferring a Finset doesn't work and is bad?

I am not an expert in this corner of the library, I don't dare to say what "the" correct approach is. I suggested an approach which to me seemed less painful than doing a finset dance. Certainly you could make a Finset with the same elements, and then create a hypothesis saying that x is in this finset, and then fin_cases would work.

As for your other question, all I'm saying is that Lean knows that D_4 has a Fintype instance, but that in type theory Sets and Finsets are different things.

"inferring a Finset" doesn't work here because the (1) fin_cases doesn't even try to do this (I guess no one thought of teaching it how to do that) and (2) 1 •> H.carrier contains H, which typeclass doesn't know anything about

· intro hx
      simp [h1, mem_zpowers_iff_mem_range_orderOf] at hx
      obtain ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩ := hx
      interval_cases a <;> grind
      done

works.

fin_cases doesn't even try to do this (I guess no one thought of teaching it how to do that)

Hm. fin_cases definitely does try to infer Fintype; the documentation allows for hypotheses "of the form h : A, where [Fintype A] is available".

Fintype appears to derive from Finset (in a broad sense of 'derive'; one of the Fintype structure's fields is a Finset), so inferring a Fintype automatically creates an appropriate Finset. Right? These appear to be fundamentally the same problem.

In the example here, actually constructing the set means knowing the definition of H supplied by h1, which is awkward. And it probably (?) also requires a theorem about ZMod. But in general I don't see why there's a difference between inferring Fintype and inferring Finset.

I've had difficulties before with Finset.prod where I was advised to stop using Fintype instances to make it work, and complained that if you write a Finset.prod and get a typing error, the error asks you to provide Fintype rather than Finset. If providing Finset is preferable, I wish the error messages would ask you to do that.

Michael said:

fin_cases doesn't even try to do this (I guess no one thought of teaching it how to do that)

Hm. fin_cases definitely does try to infer Fintype; the documentation allows for hypotheses "of the form h : A, where [Fintype A] is available".

Fintype appears to derive from Finset (in a broad sense of 'derive'; one of the Fintype structure's fields is a Finset), so inferring a Fintype automatically creates an appropriate Finset. Right? These appear to be fundamentally the same problem.

In the example here, actually constructing the set means knowing the definition of H supplied by h1, which is awkward. And it probably (?) also requires a theorem about ZMod. But in general I don't see why there's a difference between inferring Fintype and inferring Finset.

Yes, fin_cases will try to derive a Fintype instance if you fin_cases x, but it won't try to do the same when you fin_cases hx.

Kevin Buzzard said:

simp [h1, mem_zpowers_iff_mem_range_orderOf] at hx changes it to hx : ∃ a < 4, DihedralGroup.r ↑a = x.

Well, that's true, but it relies on the theorem that 1 • s = s for all s. (Interestingly, this appears to be an axiom of the MulAction class.) Following this advice would leave me not knowing how to complete other extremely similar proofs.

For example, if I substitute DihedralGroup.r 2 for 1 in the goal, it remains just as true, but in that case simp fails to simplify the hypothesis because there is no axiom about what happens when you do a pointwise action with DihedralGroup.r 2.

I was hoping for logic more along the lines of "a∙S={ax∣x∈S}a \bullet S = \left\{ ax \mid x \in S \right\}a∙S={ax∣x∈S} for all aaa", with the four cases being x = 1 * DihedralGroup.r 0, x = 1 * DihedralGroup.r 1, etc. rather than x = DihedralGroup.r 1, x = DihedralGroup.r 2, etc.
you can use docs#Set.mem_smul_set
